States that self-hosted gateway and in-house build tie on control and on compliance cost, because both keep event data on the platform's own infrastructure.
States that thin payloads move the versioning question to the API call the consumer subsequently makes.
Declines to recommend adopting CloudEvents unless the platform must interoperate with an event mesh that already speaks it.
Documents config-change propagation lag, a subscription edit taking a minute or two to reach the delivery path, as expected behavior rather than a bug.
Specifies delivery logs filterable by endpoint, event type, and status.
Surfaces exhausted deliveries as incidents grouped by endpoint and status code with notification, rather than as rows in a queue behind a bare replay button.
Documents the 200-then-crash blackhole: a handler that acknowledges then throws has reported success, and no debugging surface can see inside it.
States that a design good enough for the most sophisticated consumer segment still fails no-code consumers, because the consumer segments do not nest.
States that four of five rubric elements is a fail, not a pass.

without_skill.expectation: Explains that a subscriber which processes an event then crashes before returning 200 will receive that event again.
States that offerings marketed as exactly-once are at-least-once plus deduplication tooling.
States that the per-event ID must ship from day one, because retrofitting it later cannot help subscribers who already built without it.
States best-effort, non-guaranteed ordering as the position on the page instead of promising ordering.
Gives retries and parallel delivery workers as the reason ordering cannot be guaranteed.
Offers FIFO only as an explicit opt-in for subscribers who structurally cannot tolerate reordering, never as the platform default.
Warns subscribers not to infer event order from event timestamps.
Recommends adopting the Standard Webhooks spec rather than keeping a bespoke scheme.
Specifies the three delivery headers webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, and webhook-signature.
Gives the signed content as {id}.{timestamp}.{raw_body}, with literal dot separators.
Specifies base64 encoding of the HMAC-SHA256 output rather than the current hex encoding.
Specifies that the signature header carries multiple space-delimited signatures so the old and new secrets validate simultaneously during a rotation window.
Gives an ordered rotation flow in which the old secret is revoked only after delivery success under the new secret is confirmed.
Offers asymmetric ed25519 signing as an additional mode, naming the whsk_/whpk_ key prefixes or the v1a signature identifier, for consumers who should not hold a shared secret.
Tells the docs to instruct consumers to exempt the webhook route from session-auth middleware, since the route authenticates by signature.
Tells the docs to require signature verification on every request without exception, including notification-only handlers.
Recommends a fixed exponential-backoff schedule spanning roughly a day as the default.
Cites at least one documented vendor schedule as the reference for that span, such as Svix's 8 attempts over about 27.5 hours or Stripe's up to 3 days.
Says to size the total retry span against realistic subscriber incident durations, contrasting a deploy taking minutes against an outage taking hours, rather than picking a round number.
Rejects retrying non-retriable 4xx responses and routes them straight to the dead-letter queue.
Gives dead-lettering exactly two triggers: the retry budget being exhausted, and a non-retriable error class.

Gives the reason for deleting rather than demoting: an option parked at the bottom on a compliance ground reappears as scope the next time a deadline bites, without the legal review that ruled it out.
Names the re-promotion trigger that would put the managed option back on the menu: a signed DPA plus a data-residency posture covering the vendor.
Recommends a self-hosted open-source webhook gateway as the choice under this constraint.
States that self-hosted gateway and in-house build tie on control and on compliance cost, because both keep event data on the platform's own infrastructure.
Ranks in-house build as the highest-effort option and names what would promote it, such as webhook delivery being the product sold or third-party code also being ruled out.
Cites the order-of-magnitude in-house estimate as engineer-years rather than engineer-weeks, on the order of 3-5 engineers for 6-12 months plus a standing on-call.
Flags that engineer-years figure as a vendor's own self-interested estimate while accepting its order of magnitude.
Ties the seven-week hard date explicitly into the ranking, promoting the faster-to-effect option.
States that buying or self-hosting the delivery machinery does not buy the event taxonomy, the delivery contract, or the documentation, all of which still have to be designed.
States that the ranking is a default to be re-ranked against the team's actual situation, not a law.
Rejects splitting the event name across an HTTP header and a body field, on the grounds that no single string then names the event.
Prescribes the Object-Action resource.action pattern, dot-delimited.
Restricts event identifiers to the [a-zA-Z0-9_.] character set.
Attributes the dot-delimited past-tense resource.action convention to Standard Webhooks and/or Stripe.
Answers the bubbling question by requiring an explicit documented decision rather than defaulting to firing all three events.
Cites Stripe's position that subresource events never bubble to parent events, for example that customer.subscription.updated fires no customer.updated.
States that leaving the bubbling rule unstated breeds subscriber assumptions.
Requires every event type to have a stable name, a description, and a payload schema before it ships.
Checks events against the five design principles by name: self-contained, immutable, traceable, actionable, debuggable.
Requires choosing exactly one schema-versioning camp deliberately, and warns against drifting into both by accident.
Describes the first camp as pinning each webhook endpoint to an API version and rendering payloads per that version, attributed to Stripe.
Describes the second camp as versioning the event type itself, with a new type name per breaking change and additive-only evolution otherwise, attributed to Svix or Standard Webhooks.
Says the delivery log must be built to store headers from day one rather than retrofitted.
Raises thin payloads as a first-class alternative and states that a thin payload never changes shape when the API version bumps.
States that thin payloads move the versioning question to the API call the consumer subsequently makes.
Cites the recommendation to keep payloads small, roughly under 20kb.
Offers the dual-run migration pattern for a full-to-thin move: emit both event flavors during the transition with a discriminator field so consumers can dual-run idempotently.
Recommends documenting the outbound events in the same OpenAPI document as the inbound API, using OpenAPI 3.1's webhooks section.
Declines to recommend adopting CloudEvents unless the platform must interoperate with an event mesh that already speaks it.
Defines paused as subscriber-initiated and disabled as platform-initiated after sustained failure.
Warns that recreating a subscription under the same name restarts from the default position, so the subscriber silently loses or double-replays a backlog.
Specifies two independently configured replay positions: where a newly created subscription starts, and where a subscription resumes after a platform-side incident.
States that those two replay positions can legitimately differ, and that both must be specified.
Keeps the two filtering axes independent: event type selected against the catalog, and recipient or channel scoping.
States that an endpoint with no filter configured receives everything, and that this must be documented explicitly.
Documents config-change propagation lag, a subscription edit taking a minute or two to reach the delivery path, as expected behavior rather than a bug.
Rejects treating a customer-facing consumer portal as a phase-2 nice-to-have, and states that the portal is table stakes in this market.
Specifies delivery logs filterable by endpoint, event type, and status.
Specifies per-attempt inspection covering request headers, request body, response code, and timing.
Defines replay as re-ingesting the original as a new event.
Offers both single-event and range replay, gating a large replay window behind an explicit cost confirmation.
Surfaces exhausted deliveries as incidents grouped by endpoint and status code with notification, rather than as rows in a queue behind a bare replay button.
